Write a program that prints exactly `Hello, World!`.
Use the print() function.
Text must be inside quotes, and capitals and punctuation must match exactly.
print() displays whatever you give it. Quotes mark the text as a string.
Create a variable called `language` holding the text `Python`, then print the variable.
Use = to store a value: name = value
Print the variable without quotes.
The = sign stores the string in the variable; print(language) shows what is inside it.
Read two whole numbers, each on its own line, and print their sum.
input() returns text — convert it with int().
Read the second number the same way, then print(a + b).
Each input() reads one line. int() turns the text into a number so + adds instead of joining.
Read a name and print `My name is <name>`.
Store input() in a variable.
Use an f-string: f"My name is {name}"
f-strings insert the variable's value where the braces are.
Given `x = 3.5`, print the name of its type (just `float`, not `<class 'float'>`).
type(x) gives the class.
The class has a __name__ attribute.
type(x) returns the class float; .__name__ gives its name as a string.
Read an integer. Print `Positive`, `Negative` or `Zero`.
Use if / elif / else.
Check n > 0 first, then n < 0.
Three cases need if, elif and else. Zero is neither positive nor negative, so it goes in else.
Read two integers (two lines) and print the larger. If they are equal, print `Equal`.
Compare with > and ==.
Handle the equal case explicitly.
Checking equality first keeps the other branches simple.
Read width and height (decimals allowed, two lines). Print the area rounded to 2 decimals.
0 < width, height ≤ 1000
Use float(input()).
Format with f"{area:.2f}".
Area = width × height. The :.2f format shows exactly two decimals.
Read a line of text and print how many characters it has **not counting spaces**.
len() counts characters.
Remove spaces first with .replace(" ", "").
replace removes every space, then len counts what is left.
Read n and print its multiplication table from 1 to 10 in the format `n x i = result`.
for i in range(1, 11):
print(f"{n} x {i} = {n * i}")
range(1, 11) produces 1 to 10; each iteration prints one line of the table.
Read n and print all even numbers from 2 to n (inclusive) on one line separated by spaces.
range(2, n + 1, 2)
print(*range(...)) prints items separated by spaces.
A step of 2 starting from 2 gives only even numbers; * unpacks them into print.
Read numbers on one line separated by spaces and print their sum and average (1 decimal).
list(map(int, input().split()))
sum(nums) / len(nums)
split breaks the line into pieces, map(int, ...) converts each, sum and len do the rest.
Read a line of text and print it reversed. Then on the next line print `Palindrome` if the text (ignoring case and spaces) reads the same backwards, otherwise `Not palindrome`.
text[::-1] reverses a string.
For the check, compare clean == clean[::-1] where clean = text.replace(" ", "").lower().
Slicing with step -1 walks the string backwards. Normalising case and spaces makes the palindrome check fair.
Read numbers on one line. Print the values that appear more than once, sorted ascending, separated by spaces. If none, print `None`.
Track numbers you've seen in a set.
When you see a number again, add it to a duplicates set.
Sets give fast membership checks. A second sighting means a duplicate; sets also prevent listing it twice.
Read a sentence. Count each word (case-insensitive) and print `word: count` lines sorted by count (highest first), then alphabetically for ties.
counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
A dictionary maps each word to its count. Sorting by (-count, word) gives highest counts first and alphabetical ties.
Read numbers on one line and print the second-largest **distinct** value. If it does not exist, print `None`.
Remove duplicates with set().
Sort the unique values and take [-2].
Duplicates of the maximum would otherwise be counted as 'second largest'; a set removes them.
Read an expression like `12 * 4` (number, operator, number separated by spaces) and print the result. Support `+ - * /`. Print integers without `.0`. For division by zero print `Error`.
a, op, b = input().split()
If result == int(result), print int(result).
Converting to float supports decimals; the final check prints whole numbers neatly.
Read n. For each number 1..n print `Fizz` if divisible by 3, `Buzz` if by 5, `FizzBuzz` if by both, else the number.
Check divisible by 15 (both) first.
Use % to test divisibility.
Order matters: test the most specific case (15) first, or it would print Fizz instead of FizzBuzz.
Read a line and print how many times each vowel (a, e, i, o, u) appears, case-insensitive, as `a:X e:X i:X o:X u:X`.
text.lower().count(v)
str.count counts occurrences; a generator inside join builds the line.
Read words on one line. Group words that are anagrams of each other. Print each group on its own line: words sorted alphabetically and joined by spaces; groups ordered by their first word.
Two words are anagrams if sorted(word) is equal.
Use "".join(sorted(w)) as a dictionary key.
Sorting letters gives every anagram the same signature, which becomes the dict key grouping them.
Read a string containing `()[]{}` and other characters. Print `Balanced` if every bracket is closed in the correct order, else `Not balanced`.
Use a list as a stack: push opening brackets.
On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner.
A stack remembers the most recent unclosed bracket. Leftover items at the end mean something was never closed.
Read n (2 ≤ n ≤ 100000) and print how many primes are ≤ n, then the largest one. Use an efficient method — a slow solution may time out.
Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark multiples of each prime as not prime.
Start crossing out from p*p.
The sieve crosses out multiples instead of testing each number separately, running in roughly n log log n time.
Read r and c on the first line, then r lines of c integers. Print the transposed matrix (c lines of r integers).
Read rows into a list of lists.
zip(*matrix) transposes.
zip(*m) takes the i-th item of every row together — exactly the i-th column.
Read a string and compress runs of the same character: `aaabcc` → `a3b1c2`. Then print the original length and the compressed length on a second line as `X -> Y`.
Track the current character and a counter.
When the character changes, append char+count.
The inner loop finds the end of each run; its length is j - i.
Read a sorted list of integers on line 1 and a target on line 2. Print the index of the target using binary search, or `-1`. On a second line print how many comparisons you made.
Keep low and high indexes; check the middle each step.
Count one comparison per middle check.
Each step halves the search space, so even a million items need only about 20 comparisons.
